name: Dasapushpam
tagline: The ten sacred herbs of Karkidakam — seasonal, medicinal and cultural
summary: Dasapushpam are the ten small, common herbs Keralites honour in the Malayalam month of Karkidakam (mid‑July–mid‑August); they appear in rituals, pookalams and Karkidaka Kanji and have traditional…
description: Dasapushpam (from Sanskrit dasha = ten, pushpam = flowers) is the traditional Kerala grouping of ten small herbs valued for ritual, seasonal health and folk medicine. People display them in household shrines, wear them in Thiruvathira and use them in Karkidaka Kanji during the monsoon month of Karkidakam.

The plants are common roadside and field herbs across Kerala; though called ‘flowers’ the medicinal and cultural value usually lies in the whole plant or leaves. Each herb traditionally links to a deity and to specific protective or therapeutic uses in local belief.

Modern reviews and local Ayurvedic practice document antimicrobial, anti‑inflammatory and other bioactivities for many Dashapushpam members, and hospitals that run Karkidaka chikitsa include them as seasonal ingredients (always under physician guidance).

For a visitor, Dasapushpam is best experienced during Karkidakam (roughly July 16–August 15): look for displays at temples, family shrines, herbal gardens and Ayurveda centres, and taste supervised Karkidaka Kanji at reputable clinics. Confirm any medicinal use with a qualified practitioner before trying.
highlights: A set of ten small, common herbs honoured in Kerala’s Karkidakam month
Used in household shrines, pookalams and the seasonal Karkidaka Kanji
Each plant has folklore deity associations and traditional health roles
Many members have been studied for antimicrobial, anti‑inflammatory and other activities
Best observed in monsoon (Karkidakam) when plants are fresh
Seen across Kerala — temple grounds, home gardens, Ayurvedic hospitals

sections.heading: Background
body: Dasapushpam is a Kerala cultural‑botanical grouping: ten herbs traditionally gathered and displayed during the Malayalam month of Karkidakam (the rainy month). The practice appears in household ritual (display on a brass plate, wearing small garlands) and seasonal health customs described in local texts and folk practice. Sources note the custom of wearing or ‘keeping warm’ the Dasapushpam through Karkidakam to gain protective benefits for the year.

sections.heading: The ten plants (common and botanical names)
body: Different local lists exist but standard, widely cited members of Dasapushpam are: Cardiospermum halicacabum (uzhinja / balloon vine), Eclipta alba (kayyonni / bhringaraja), Cynodon dactylon (karuka / durva), Evolvulus alsinoides (vishnukranthi / slender dwarf morning‑glory), Aerva lanata (cheroola), Biophytum sensitivum (mukkutti), Emilia sonchifolia (muyal cheviyan), Vernonia cinerea or Cyanthillium cinereum (poovamkurunnila / little ironweed), Ipomoea sepiaria (thiruthaali) and Curculigo orchioides (nilappana / black musali).

Although Malayalam names often refer to flowers, the cultural and therapeutic emphasis is usually on leaves or the whole plant. Regional lists and names vary slightly; consult local signage or an herbarium guide when identifying plants in the field.

sections.heading: Cultural use and therapeutic role
body: Dasapushpam features in multiple Kerala customs: Athapookalam and Thiruvathira adornment, display in shrines during Karkidakam and as part of Karkidaka Kanji — a medicated rice porridge used in monsoon seasonal care. Traditional sources link each herb to a presiding deity and to specific ritual benefits.

Contemporary Ayurvedic and pharmacological studies report a range of bioactivities (antimicrobial, anti‑inflammatory, antioxidant and more) for many of the plants in the group; modern practitioners include fresh Dashapushpam herbs among ingredients when preparing Karkidaka Kanji, but emphasise physician supervision for therapeutic use.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Best time: visit in Karkidakam (roughly July 16–August 15) to see fresh Dasapushpam displays, temple rituals and Karkidaka Kanji programmes. Many Ayurvedic hospitals and heritage museums or botanical gardens run seasonal demonstrations or Karkidaka chikitsa packages.

Where to look: check temple precincts, local home shrines, village herbal gardens and Ayurveda centres (Kannur, Thrissur, Palakkad and other districts have active seasonal programmes). If you wish to sample Karkidaka Kanji or join a Karkidaka Chikitsa programme, book with an accredited Ayurvedic hospital or centre and follow medical guidance.

latest.text: Wikipedia Dasapushpam entry was updated (Sept 25, 2026) with an up‑to‑date list and references summarising botanical names and cultural notes.

A March–April 2026 review links Dasapushpam and the practice of wearing medicinal flowers to classical 'Puṣpayurveda' ideas and modern phytochemical evidence, discussing fragrance‑mediated effects and chronotherapy.
Malayala Manorama piece (July 15, 2025) described continuing household Karkidakam rituals: lighting lamps, placing Dasapushpam before the lamp and the deity associations for each herb.

visitorInfo.bestTime: Karkidakam (roughly mid‑July to mid‑August), immediately after monsoon showers when herbs are fresh
visitorInfo.howToReach: Dasapushpam is state‑wide — find plants in temple grounds, village gardens and herbal parks across Kerala; reach major Kerala towns (Kochi, Thiruvananthapuram, Kannur, Thrissur) by road/rail/air and ask local guides or Ayurveda centres for seasonal displays and Karkidaka Kanji programmes.
etiquette: Do not harvest or ingest wild herbs without guidance — consult an Ayurvedic practitioner or local expert before use.
Respect temple and household rituals — ask permission before photographing or touching shrine displays.
Bring a local plant‑ID guide or use a botanical app; Malayalam common names vary by district.
Support sustainable use: avoid uprooting rare plants and favour visits to botanical gardens or accredited Ayurveda centres for demonstrations.
